answer.question: Where should a putting green go in an established Applewood yard?
answer.answer: Look for usable putting lines, a convenient route from the house and room to stand. Keep existing trees and roots in the plan, and consider leaf cleanup. We can compare the green with lawn or pet-turf options during the free visit.

blocks.h2: Useful putting lines come before extra cups.
paras: Choose the distances you want to work on and whether chipping matters to you. A green near the patio may get more use than a larger one at the far end of the yard. Leave walking room around it and keep beds or other garden features that you enjoy.

blocks.h2: Plan around what has been there for years.
paras: On a tree-lined Applewood property, mark mature trees, roots and irrigation before discussing preparation. Avoid assuming that an open patch above ground is clear for excavation below it. Point out settled paving or known wet areas as well.

If reducing lawn irrigation is part of your decision, check the provider on your bill and compare your own costs. Allow for turf cleaning, especially for pets, and confirm any rebate eligibility before counting it in the budget.

blocks.h2: A golf course inside Applewood, and room for a green at home.
paras: Applewood has its own course. Applewood Golf Course, at 14001 W. 32nd Ave, is a par-71 layout under the foothills that has been open since the 1960s, managed by KemperSports and open daily from 6 a.m. to sunset (Applewood Golf Course). It's associated with the Prospect Recreation and Park District.
Rolling Hills Country Club, a private club, sits immediately west in Golden, and Fossil Trace Golf Club, the City of Golden's course at 3050 Illinois St, opened in 2003 (Fossil Trace Golf Club).

With a course this close, a backyard green earns its space: several holes, contour to read, and a collar of longer turf for chipping. On a flat Applewood lot it goes down without the cut-and-fill a slope would need.

blocks.h2: Water is billed in three tiers now, and the top one is $11 a thousand gallons.
paras: Applewood's water comes from Consolidated Mutual Water Company, a customer-owned utility serving since 1926 across about 24 square miles and some 100,000 people, through about 400 miles of pipe in parts of Lakewood, Wheat Ridge and unincorporated central Jefferson County. Applewood is named on its service map, where Lakewood and Wheat Ridge appear only in part (Consolidated Mutual Water). A neighbor in Wheat Ridge or Lakewood has to check the name on the bill before copying anyone's watering rules. In Applewood that part is already settled.

Its homepage says that, because of drought, allowed irrigation ends on 1 October 2026. Moderate-to-severe drought, below-normal snowpack and low reservoirs are behind the call, and a Drought Management Plan sets the rules (Consolidated Mutual Water).

That plan reached the bill first. Since 1 June 2026 Consolidated has billed monthly in three tiers, and on the standard one-ERU allotment they run $5.60 per thousand gallons for the first 5,000, $8.00 from 5,001 to 15,000, and $11.00 above 15,000 — each step costing more, the company says, “to promote conservation and to support the additional load on our water system” (Consolidated Mutual Water). Your own tier lines move with the shares attached to your tap, so ask Consolidated how many you hold. Turf drinks none of it.

As of September 2026 the company's published drought response puts it in Drought Stage Orange, the second of five steps that run Yellow, Orange, Red, Brown, Black. Orange targets a 25% cut and caps irrigation at two days a week, with no outdoor watering between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day; vegetables, flowers, trees and shrubs may still be hand-watered with a shut-off nozzle, or dripped, on any day inside those hours (Consolidated Mutual Water). Consolidated buys wholesale from Denver Water and has to align with its restrictions, and it says both pricing and enforcement may change again if conditions worsen.

blocks.h2: Flat terrace ground over Front Range clay.
paras: Applewood sits on flat to gently sloping Clear Creek terrace deposits east of South Table Mountain, with none of the hogback or steep bedrock found farther south. The clay under it is still Front Range clay, which the Colorado Geological Survey calls Colorado's most significant geologic hazard and blames for more property damage than any other natural hazard (Colorado Geological Survey).

So the base decides the rest. On a flat, open yard the turf itself goes down in wide pieces with fewer seams; what takes the time is underneath, getting the depth and the fall right for whatever the ground turns out to be when it is opened.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Applewood, CO?
faq.a: We install backyard putting greens, artificial lawns and pet turf in Applewood, CO, where Applewood Golf Course sits at 32nd Avenue and Youngfield Street. Consolidated Mutual Water, Applewood's utility, ends allowed irrigation for 2026 on 1 October because of drought. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: Do I need a Jefferson County permit for artificial turf in Applewood?
faq.a: For a normal yard, no. Jefferson County requires a grading permit once the disturbed area exceeds half an acre, 21,780 square feet (Jefferson County), which is far more ground than a back-yard green or lawn turns over. A yard project matches none of the named rows on the County's land-disturbance flyer, so it falls to the catch-all, “Anything Else”, where under 0.5 acre the permit column reads “None*” — and the asterisk sends you to Section 16 of the Zoning Resolution, whose performance standards you have to meet either way (Jefferson County). Applewood is unincorporated, so the office to ask is County Planning and Zoning, on 303-271-8700.

faq.q: Can an HOA stop turf in an Applewood back yard?
faq.a: Most Applewood subdivisions predate HOAs, so many addresses don't have one. Where covenants exist, a detached home's back yard is protected: SB23-178 bars HOA design rules from prohibiting nonvegetative turf there (SB23-178). Front yards aren't covered, so read your covenants before planning one.

faq.q: Can I get a water rebate for turf in Applewood?
faq.a: Don't count on one. Water-wise rebates around the metro fund living plants, and Colorado's own turf-replacement grants barred artificial turf before they closed in March 2025 (CWCB). The rebate rules, provider by provider, are in our guide.

faq.q: Where does Applewood start and stop?
faq.a: South Table Mountain forms the western edge; Fairmount lies north, Wheat Ridge northeast, Lakewood southeast and West Pleasant View southwest (Applewood). Locals find their way by 32nd Avenue, the golf course and the mountain, with Maple Grove Park and its reservoir, the Clear Creek trail and the Applewood Village shops close by.

faq.q: Will turf work under Applewood’s old trees?
faq.a: That is often where it earns its place. This was orchard ground before it was divided into lots, and the canopy that grew up since leaves shade patches where grass has already given up. Turf needs no sun; see how shade changes turf’s surface temperature. Roots are the real constraint, and the free site visit maps them before any digging.
